name: Déjérine-Roussy thalamic pain syndrome
vascularTerritory: Often ventral-posterior thalamic inferolateral/PCA branches, but central post-stroke pain can arise from other somatosensory pathway lesions.
presentation: Thalamic sensory injury can cause contralateral sensory loss, sometimes followed by neuropathic pain, allodynia or hyperpathia. Pain may be delayed and does not develop after every thalamic lesion. Sensory ataxia or other associated findings depend on the affected pathways.
cause: A thalamic form of central post-stroke pain related to somatosensory pathway injury. VPL/VPM are primary somatosensory relays; pulvinar is not substituted as the primary somatosensory relay.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, thalamic somatosensory relays and thalamic pain, printed pp. 284-288 (PDF pp. 310-314).

name: Artery-of-Percheron paramedian thalamic infarction
vascularTerritory: A variant single paramedian artery, usually from one PCA P1 segment, supplying both paramedian thalami with variable rostral midbrain territory.
presentation: Bilateral paramedian infarcts may cause impaired arousal, memory dysfunction and vertical gaze abnormalities, with variable other signs. MRI patterns include bilateral paramedian thalamic involvement with or without midbrain and sometimes anterior thalamic extension. A midbrain V sign may occur; a Y-shaped lesion is not a defining sign.
cause: Occlusion of an artery-of-Percheron variant. Midbrain involvement and the classic clinical triad are variable.
refs: Lazzaro et al., Artery of Percheron Infarction: Imaging Patterns and Clinical Spectrum, AJNR 2010;31:1283-1289, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20299438/.
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 18, bilateral medial diencephalic memory lesions, printed pp. 842 (PDF pp. 868).

name: Tuberothalamic artery syndrome (aphasia-plus)
vascularTerritory: Tuberothalamic (polar) artery usually arises from posterior communicating artery; it can be absent with supply replaced by adjacent paramedian branches.
presentation: Anterior/anteromedial thalamic injury can cause memory and executive/behavioral dysfunction. Dominant-hemisphere lesions may have language deficits and nondominant lesions neglect, with considerable individual and territorial variation. No fixed aphasia-plus or tremor pattern is required.
cause: Infarction affecting variable anterior nuclear, mammillothalamic and associated thalamofrontal territories.
refs: Schmahmann, Vascular Syndromes of the Thalamus, Stroke 2003;34:2264-2278, https://doi.org/10.1161/01.STR.0000087786.38997.9E (origins and variable arterial territories).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 18, diencephalic memory circuits, printed pp. 836-843 (PDF pp. 862-869).

name: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
vascularTerritory: Thiamine-deficiency disorder, not a vascular territory.
presentation: Wernicke encephalopathy may cause mental-status/memory change, ocular motor abnormalities and ataxia; the full classic triad is frequently incomplete. Korsakoff syndrome refers to persistent severe memory impairment, sometimes with confabulation and executive dysfunction. The two are related but not compulsory sequential phases in every patient. MRI findings vary with acuity and may be absent.
cause: Thiamine deficiency in settings including alcohol use disorder, inadequate nutrition, prolonged vomiting or other malabsorptive/medical conditions. Medial diencephalic, mammillary and additional periventricular networks can be affected.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 18, Wernicke-Korsakoff and memory circuits, printed pp. 842-843 (PDF pp. 868-869).
Galvin et al., EFNS guidelines for diagnosis, therapy and prevention of Wernicke encephalopathy, 2010, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20642790/.

name: Hypothalamic dysfunction
vascularTerritory: Variable hypothalamic branches of ICA/ACA/posterior communicating/PCA systems; many cases are nonvascular.
presentation: Hypothalamic or stalk disease may disturb water balance, endocrine regulation, appetite/energy balance, temperature, sleep or autonomic control. Vasopressin deficiency causes dilute polyuria, with hypernatremia particularly when water intake is inadequate. SIADH and paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity have many causes and do not uniquely identify isolated hypothalamic nuclei.
cause: Tumor, surgery/trauma, inflammatory/infiltrative disease or vascular injury involving hypothalamic and pituitary-stalk networks. Symptoms depend on lesion extent and are not a fixed nuclear checklist.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, hypothalamic nuclei and regional functions, printed pp. 792-797 (PDF pp. 818-823).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, water balance, printed pp. 803-804 (PDF pp. 829-830).

name: Pineal region tumor with gaze palsy
vascularTerritory: Regional mass effect or other nonvascular disease; obstructive hydrocephalus can accompany aqueduct compression.
presentation: Pineal-region disease may cause dorsal midbrain gaze abnormalities and raised intracranial pressure if CSF flow is obstructed. Individual Parinaud features and hydrocephalus are variable. Some hCG-secreting germ-cell tumors can cause precocious puberty, particularly in boys; this is not a universal property of germinoma.
cause: Pineal parenchymal or germ-cell tumors and other pineal-region lesions. Compression of posterior commissural/pretectal circuits or aqueduct explains associated manifestations but is not required for every lesion.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, dorsal midbrain gaze syndrome, printed pp. 587-588 (PDF pp. 613-614).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 5, pineal-region mass with hydrocephalus, printed pp. 203-204 (PDF pp. 229-230).
National Cancer Institute, Childhood CNS Germ Cell Tumors Treatment (PDQ), https://www.cancer.gov/types/brain/hp/child-cns-germ-cell-treatment-pdq.

name: Hemiballismus
vascularTerritory: May result from contralateral subthalamic or other basal-ganglia network lesions; vascular supply depends on the actual lesion site.
presentation: Large-amplitude irregular flinging movements, predominantly proximal and unilateral, often coexist with chorea. Additional deficits and evolution vary; lack of weakness or sensory loss is possible but not required.
cause: Contralateral subthalamic injury is a classic mechanism, but other basal-ganglia lesions also cause hemichorea/hemiballismus. Hyperglycemia-associated cases frequently involve striatum rather than STN. Motor-network imbalance is more informative than a one-nucleus-only rule.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 16, basal-ganglia pathways and hemiballismus, printed pp. 748-755 (PDF pp. 774-781).
Characterization of Diabetic Chorea in 20 Patients, 2016, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27536463/.
